opus-5.5.text:
I think it really comes down to the structure of the environment and the variability of the task. In a factory, you can engineer the world around the robot. The parts arrive in the same orientation, the lighting is controlled, the cycle is the same thousands of times a day. So you can get away with something fairly narrow: a well-tuned controller, maybe a learned policy for a specific skill, and the "reasoning" is mostly done upfront by the engineers who designed the cell.

A home is basically the opposite of that. Every house is different, the layout changes, people move things around, there are kids and pets, objects the robot has never seen before. And the tasks themselves are open-ended. If someone says "clean up the living room," that's not one skill, it's a long sequence of decisions: what counts as clutter, where does this object belong, should I move the chair to get under the table, what do I do if the cup is still half full. You can't enumerate all of those cases in advance.

So you need a layer that can generalize at a more abstract level: understanding semantics, breaking a vague instruction into sub-goals, recovering when something goes wrong. That's where these larger vision-language style models come in, sitting on top of the lower-level control. From my side, coming from locomotion and reinforcement learning, I'd say the low-level skills are getting quite robust now. We can make robots walk, balance, and manipulate pretty reliably in simulation and transfer that to the real world. The bottleneck in the home is much more about deciding what to do and in what order, and adapting that on the fly, rather than how to physically execute a single motion.

There's also a practical economic angle. In industry, you can amortize a lot of custom engineering over a huge number of repetitions. In the home, nobody is going to pay an integrator to program their kitchen. The robot has to figure it out itself, and that pretty much forces you toward more general, more abstract reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response says industrial tasks are repetitive and that their reasoning is handled upfront by engineers who design the cell, conveying that instructions can be made concrete in advance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key difference is really about the variability of the environment. In an industrial setting, you can engineer the environment around the robot. The parts arrive in the same place, in the same orientation, the lighting is controlled, nothing unexpected walks into the workcell. So the robot doesn't really need to understand what it's doing, it just needs to execute a very precise motion over and over, and if something is off, you stop and a human fixes it.

In a home, you have none of that. Every house is different, every kitchen is laid out differently, objects get moved around, there are kids and pets, there's clutter. The robot might get asked to do something it's never seen in exactly that form before, like "put the groceries away," which means figuring out what's in the bag, where things go in this particular kitchen, that milk goes in the fridge but cereal doesn't, and so on. You can't pre-program all of that. You need some level of understanding of the task and the world, the ability to decompose a vague instruction into steps, and to recover when something goes wrong, like a cabinet that's stuck or an object that falls.

So that's where the more abstract reasoning comes in. And I think of it as a hierarchy. At the low level, for locomotion and basic manipulation, reinforcement learning and sim-to-real work really well, and that's a lot of what I've focused on. You can train very robust controllers in simulation for walking over difficult terrain or handling contacts. But those policies are relatively narrow. They don't know what a kitchen is. What you need on top is something that can take the long-horizon, semantic part of the problem, understanding the instruction, the context, the common sense of a household, and break it down into things the low-level controllers can actually execute. And that's where things like large language and vision-language models have become really interesting, because they bring that general world knowledge that we simply couldn't get from training in simulation alone.

r001.rationale: The response says industrial robots work in engineered, predictable environments and repeatedly execute precise motions. It does not explain that abstract instructions can be translated into concrete instructions in advance.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difference is how much you can specify in advance. In an industrial setting, you can structure the environment around the robot. The objects are in known locations, and the robot repeats a fairly well-defined task. It still needs good control, but it doesn't necessarily need to understand the broader context of what it's doing.

In a home, that context changes constantly. If you ask a robot to clean the kitchen, that's not a precise sequence of movements. It has to figure out what needs cleaning, where things belong, and how to break that goal into actions. And if something isn't where it expected, it needs to adapt.

So you need reasoning at a more abstract level to connect a human's request to concrete physical skills. The challenge is grounding that reasoning in what the robot can actually perceive and do. Having a sensible plan is only useful if the robot can execute it and recognize when it needs to change that plan.

r001.rationale: The response says industrial tasks take place in structured environments and are well-defined, but it does not explain that abstract instructions can be translated into concrete instructions in advance.

sol-6.1.text:
In an industrial setting, you can structure the environment around the robot. You know where the parts will be, and you can design a controller to perform a particular motion reliably, over and over again. A home is much less structured. Every home is different, objects move around, and the tasks themselves can be quite loosely specified.

If you ask a robot to clean up the kitchen, that’s not a single motion. It has to interpret what you mean, identify what needs to change, and break that goal down into actions. It also has to deal with things not going as expected—maybe a door is closed or an object isn’t where it anticipated. So you need reasoning at a more abstract level to decide what to do, alongside the lower-level control that lets the robot actually execute those actions.

r001.rationale: The response says industrial tasks have structured environments and can use a controller for a particular motion, but it does not explain that abstract instructions can be translated into concrete instructions in advance.
